core: finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish, and start-to-finish relationships
outOfScope: procurement, legal, financial, staffing, or organization-specific approval advice

claims.claim: A dependency or logical relationship depicts the order in which activities are planned to start or finish in relation to one another; linked activities can be described as predecessors and successors.

In a finish-to-start relationship, the successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes; in start-to-start, the successor cannot start until the predecessor starts; and in finish-to-finish, the successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes.

A start-to-finish relationship means the successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts. It is a valid fourth combination but is unusual and may be harder to interpret than the more common relationships.
Internal dependencies connect activities within one schedule, while external dependencies connect planned work to activity, information, or events outside that schedule or project boundary.

Assumptions are planning conditions treated as true for now, whereas constraints are limits or conditions that restrict available choices. Both can explain why a dependency is recorded or why it may need review.

Recording the relationship, its rationale, owner or source, relevant assumption or constraint, and review status makes a dependency easier to examine; documentation does not control an external party or guarantee timing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The sources discuss dependencies inside detailed government and professional scheduling practices, whereas this topic is a general introductory lesson.
positions: GAO explains logic relationships as part of a detailed schedule network and discourages confusing start-to-finish use.
PMI discusses dependency types in a critical-path scheduling article, including external and discretionary dependencies.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only the high-level meanings of the four relationship types, internal versus external dependencies, and transparent documentation. It does not teach calculations, prescribe a scheduling tool, or require a particular project-control process.

unsupportedExistingClaims: A generic draft could treat every dependency as finish-to-start, confuse an external dependency with work the team controls, or imply that documenting a dependency eliminates its uncertainty.
correctionsNeeded: Uses original language and a hypothetical community-workshop example rather than source diagrams or templates.
Defines each relationship in plain language and separates logical relationships from calendar dates, estimates, and critical-path calculation.
Explains assumptions and constraints as information to record and revisit, not as promises or universal organizational rules.
rightsIssues: The PMI article was checked live and is REFERENCE_ONLY; no PMI prose, figures, or diagrams are reproduced.
The GAO Schedule Assessment Guide was checked live and is a U.S. government publication; the lesson uses original prose and reproduces no tables, figures, or procedures.
